citation_entries.sentence: Augustine, our bishop at Hippo, taught that the punishment of the lost has no end.
Augustine let the doubters suppose, if the thought gave them pleasure, that the pains of the damned are at times eased.
Augustine would not let them say the punishment ends.

raw_text: Augustine writes that Origen believed even the devil and his angels would be delivered from their torments [[cic:npnf102_augustine-city-of-god-christian-doctrine.xml:iv.XXI.17#01]] [[as:paraphrase]]. Augustine writes that the Church, not without reason, condemned Origen for this and other errors [[cic:npnf102_augustine-city-of-god-christian-doctrine.xml:iv.XXI.17#01]] [[as:paraphrase]]. Among those errors Augustine names Origen's theory of a ceaseless alternation of happiness and misery at fixed periods of ages [[cic:npnf102_augustine-city-of-god-christian-doctrine.xml:iv.XXI.17#01]] [[as:paraphrase]]. Augustine says Origen was even more indulgent than the tender-hearted Christians who suppose the lost will be delivered after a fixed term of punishment [[cic:npnf102_augustine-city-of-god-christian-doctrine.xml:iv.XXI.17#01]] [[as:paraphrase]]. Augustine, our bishop at Hippo, taught that the punishment of the lost has no end [[lpc.witness.punishment-without-end]] [[as:paraphrase]]. Augustine let the doubters suppose, if the thought gave them pleasure, that the pains of the damned are at times eased [[lpc.witness.punishment-without-end]] [[as:paraphrase]].
